analogy.p: Imagine you are told the total area of a rectangular floor tile arrangement, x² + 5x + 6 square units, and asked to find the two side lengths. Expanding is like multiplying the sides to get the area; factorising is working backwards from the area to the sides (x + 2) and (x + 3). The analogy breaks down because a real rectangle needs positive lengths, whereas algebraic factors can include negative numbers, and some areas (expressions) cannot be split into whole-number sides at all.
analogy.t: Factorising is unpacking a rectangle into its sides

bullets: Factorised form is a **product** (things multiplied); expanded form is a **sum** (things added or subtracted).
Every correct factorisation can be **checked by expanding**: if you get back the original expression, you are right. This takes 20 seconds and is worth doing in the exam.
**Fully factorised** means that no further common factor can be taken out of any bracket. The answer 2(3x + 6) is only partly factorised; the full answer is 6(x + 2).
Mark schemes usually give **M1 for a correct partial attempt** (for example, one correct bracket or a correct common factor) and **A1 for the complete correct answer**.
Factorising is used to: solve quadratic equations, simplify algebraic fractions, prove identities, and find roots and turning points of quadratic graphs.
The command word **'factorise'** means you must give the answer as a product; leaving it as an expanded sum earns no marks.
core.h: What factorising means and why it matters
core.p: To **factorise** an expression means to write it as a **product** of two or more simpler expressions, usually with brackets. It is the **exact reverse of expanding**: expanding turns 3(x + 4) into 3x + 12, while factorising turns 3x + 12 back into 3(x + 4). The Edexcel specification asks you to manipulate algebraic expressions by **factorising**, including quadratics of the form x² + bx + c (with the **difference of two squares** as a special case) and, at Higher tier, quadratics of the form ax² + bx + c. Factorising matters because a product is much easier to work with than a sum: it is the key step in solving quadratic equations, simplifying algebraic fractions and finding where graphs cross the x-axis.

bullets: For 12x + 18 the HCF of 12 and 18 is 6, so 12x + 18 = **6(2x + 3)**.
For 6x²y − 9xy²: number HCF is 3; both terms contain x and y, and the lowest power of x is x¹ and of y is y¹. So the HCF is 3xy and the answer is **3xy(2x − 3y)**.
For x² + 5x: the common factor is x, so x² + 5x = **x(x + 5)**. Note that x² ÷ x = x and 5x ÷ x = 5.
If a whole term is the common factor, a **1** must remain in the bracket: 4x + 4x² = 4x(1 + x). Forgetting the 1 is a very common error.
Check by expanding: 3xy × 2x = 6x²y and 3xy × (−3y) = −9xy², matching the original.
A negative common factor can be taken out if the leading term is negative: −2x − 6 = **−2(x + 3)**. Every sign inside the bracket flips.
Common factors can also be brackets: 3(x + 2) + y(x + 2) = **(x + 2)(3 + y)**.
Do this step first even in a quadratic: 2x² + 10x + 12 = 2(x² + 5x + 6) = 2(x + 2)(x + 3).
core.h: Step 1: always look for a common factor first
core.p: A **common factor** is a number, a letter or a power of a letter that divides exactly into every term. To factorise by taking out a common factor, find the **highest common factor (HCF)** of the terms, write it outside a bracket, and write inside the bracket what is left after dividing each term by it. Always do this before trying any other method, because it makes the numbers smaller and often turns a hard quadratic into an easy one. You must take out the **highest** common factor, including both the number part and every letter part, otherwise the expression is not fully factorised.

bullets: Example: ax + ay + bx + by. Pair as (ax + ay) + (bx + by) = a(x + y) + b(x + y) = **(x + y)(a + b)**.
Numerical example: 3x + 6 + xy + 2y = 3(x + 2) + y(x + 2) = **(x + 2)(3 + y)**.
If the second pair has a minus sign, take out a **negative** factor so the brackets match: x² + 3x − 2x − 6 = x(x + 3) − 2(x + 3) = **(x + 3)(x − 2)**.
If the two brackets do not match, try re-ordering the terms or pairing a different way before giving up.
Always check that expanding your final answer gives the original four terms.
Mark schemes award a method mark for a correct first line of pairing even if you slip later, so show every line of working.
core.p: When an expression has **four terms** and there is no single common factor, try **factorising in pairs**. Group the terms into two pairs, take out the common factor from each pair, and hope that the **same bracket** appears twice. If it does, that bracket is itself a common factor and can be taken out. This is also the engine behind the 'split the middle term' method for harder quadratics, so understanding it makes the Higher-tier method much easier to trust.

bullets: **Rule:** m × n = c (the constant term) and m + n = b (the coefficient of x).
x² + 7x + 12: pairs of 12 are 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. Only 3 + 4 = 7, so **(x + 3)(x + 4)**.
If c is **positive**, m and n have the **same sign** (both positive if b is positive, both negative if b is negative): x² − 8x + 15 = **(x − 3)(x − 5)**.
If c is **negative**, m and n have **different signs**, and the larger one takes the sign of b: x² − 5x − 14 = **(x − 7)(x + 2)** because −7 × 2 = −14 and −7 + 2 = −5.
If b = 0 there is no x term, which is the difference of two squares case (see below).
If c = 0 the quadratic has a common factor: x² − 6x = x(x − 6).
The order of the brackets does not matter, because multiplication is commutative: (x + 3)(x + 4) = (x + 4)(x + 3).
If no pair works, the quadratic does not factorise with whole numbers and a different method (completing the square or the quadratic formula) is needed.
core.h: Quadratics of the form x² + bx + c
core.p: A **quadratic expression** has x² as its highest power. When the coefficient of x² is 1, the expression x² + bx + c factorises into **(x + m)(x + n)** where the two numbers **m and n multiply to give c and add to give b**. This works because expanding (x + m)(x + n) gives x² + nx + mx + mn = x² + (m + n)x + mn, so the middle number is the sum and the last number is the product. Finding the right pair is a short search through the factor pairs of c, using the signs to decide which pair is correct.

bullets: Step 1: write the quadratic in the order x² + bx + c and note the signs of b and c.
Step 2: list factor pairs of |c| in order, for example for 12: (1, 12), (2, 6), (3, 4).
Step 3: use the sign of c to decide whether the numbers have the same or different signs.
Step 4: find the pair whose **sum (or difference) is |b|**, then give the larger number the sign of b if the signs differ.
Step 5: write the brackets and **expand to check**.

Example x² − 2x − 24: pairs of 24 are (1, 24), (2, 12), (3, 8), (4, 6). Different signs, so look for a difference of 2: 4 and 6 differ by 2. The larger (6) is negative because b is negative: **(x − 6)(x + 4)**. Check: −6 + 4 = −2 and −6 × 4 = −24. ✓
Prime constant terms give a quick pair: for x² + 8x + 7 the only pair is 1 and 7, which add to 8, so **(x + 1)(x + 7)**.
core.h: A systematic method for finding the pair of numbers
core.p: Guessing wastes time and loses marks, so use a **systematic list**. Write down all the factor pairs of the constant term c, then check which pair has the required sum b, taking the signs into account. This is an organised search that a top-grade student can do in under a minute, and writing the list in your working shows the examiner a clear method. The same table idea works for the harder ax² + bx + c case, where you list pairs of factors of **ac** instead.

bullets: **Pattern:** a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). Learn this exactly.
x² − 16 = (x + 4)(x − 4) because 16 = 4². Likewise y² − 25 = (y + 5)(y − 5).
Take out a common factor first: 2x² − 50 = 2(x² − 25) = **2(x + 5)(x − 5)**.
Repeated use: x⁴ − 81 = (x² + 9)(x² − 9) = **(x² + 9)(x + 3)(x − 3)**. The factor x² + 9 cannot be broken down further.
Mental arithmetic use: 99² − 1² = 100 × 98 = 9800, and 51² − 49² = 100 × 2 = 200.

Geometric view: take a square of side a, remove a square of side b from a corner, and rearrange the L-shape into a rectangle of sides (a + b) and (a − b); the area is the same, which is why the identity is true (see figure).
core.p: The expression a² − b² (one square number or square term **minus** another) factorises as **(a + b)(a − b)**. It is a special case of x² + bx + c in which the middle term is missing, because the two cross terms +ab and −ab **cancel**: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − ab + ab − b² = a² − b². Spotting this pattern saves a great deal of time. It only works for a **subtraction** of two perfect squares: x² + 9 does **not** factorise using real numbers.

bullets: **Step 1:** multiply a and c. For 2x² + 7x + 3, ac = 2 × 3 = 6.
**Step 2:** find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b: 1 and 6 (1 × 6 = 6 and 1 + 6 = 7).
**Step 3:** split the middle term: 2x² + x + 6x + 3.
**Step 4:** factorise in pairs: x(2x + 1) + 3(2x + 1).
**Step 5:** take out the common bracket: **(2x + 1)(x + 3)**. Expand to check: 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 2x² + 7x + 3 ✓.
With a negative constant: 3x² − 5x − 2 has ac = −6; the numbers −6 and 1 give −5; so 3x² − 6x + x − 2 = 3x(x − 2) + 1(x − 2) = **(3x + 1)(x − 2)**.
The order of the two split terms does not matter; either order gives the same final brackets.

Alternative: **trial and improvement** with brackets, writing factors of ax² in the x positions and factors of c at the ends, checking the middle term each time. It is quicker when you can see the answer, but the splitting method is more reliable.
If a is a common factor of all three terms, take it out first (6x² + 10x + 4 = 2(3x² + 5x + 2) = 2(3x + 2)(x + 1)).
core.h: Quadratics of the form ax² + bx + c (Higher tier)
core.p: When the coefficient of x² is not 1, the pair of numbers must multiply to **ac** (the product of the x² coefficient and the constant) and add to **b**. The most reliable method is to **split the middle term**: replace bx by two terms using the numbers you found, then factorise the four terms **by grouping**. The two brackets that result will be the same, and the final answer is the product of that repeated bracket and the bracket of leftover factors. This method always works if the quadratic factorises, which makes it the safest choice under exam pressure.

bullets: x² + 6x + 9 = **(x + 3)²** because 3 × 3 = 9 and 3 + 3 = 6. Likewise x² − 10x + 25 = (x − 5)².
A perfect square has **a square constant term** and a middle coefficient equal to **twice the square root** of that constant (with its sign).
(x + k)² is **not** x² + k²; you must include the middle term 2kx. This is one of the most common errors in algebra.
A perfect square quadratic touches the x-axis at one point (a **repeated root**), so the graph has its turning point on the x-axis.
Coefficients: 4x² + 12x + 9 = (2x + 3)² since (2x)² = 4x², 3² = 9 and 2 × 2x × 3 = 12x.
Completing the square: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the minimum value is −4 at x = −3.
core.h: Perfect squares and links to completing the square
core.p: A **perfect square** quadratic has the form x² + 2kx + k², which factorises as **(x + k)²**, a repeated bracket. Recognising it quickly saves time and also explains why some quadratics have only one repeated root. This pattern is the basis of **completing the square**, which writes any quadratic as (x + p)² + q and is used to find the turning point of a graph and to solve quadratics that do not factorise. At Higher tier you should be able to move comfortably between these forms.

bullets: Solve x² − x − 6 = 0: factorise to (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0, so **x = 3 or x = −2**.
The equation **must equal 0** before you factorise. For x² + 2x = 15, move the 15 first: x² + 2x − 15 = 0, giving (x + 5)(x − 3) = 0, so x = −5 or x = 3.
Never divide both sides by x: for x² = 5x, doing so loses the root x = 0. Instead write x² − 5x = 0, so x(x − 5) = 0 and **x = 0 or x = 5**.
For 3x² − 5x − 2 = 0, factorise to (3x + 1)(x − 2) = 0, so **x = −1/3 or x = 2**. Each bracket is solved separately: 3x + 1 = 0 gives x = −1/3.
Check solutions by substituting back into the original equation.
The roots of y = x² − x − 6 are the x-intercepts at (−2, 0) and (3, 0); the turning point lies halfway between them at x = 0.5.
Questions with context (areas, lengths) often have one root that is negative and must be rejected because a length cannot be negative.
core.h: Using factorising to solve quadratic equations
core.p: One of the most important uses of factorising is solving a quadratic equation. First rearrange so that **one side equals zero** (ax² + bx + c = 0), then factorise, then use the **null factor law**: if the product of two quantities is zero, then at least one of them must be zero. Set each bracket equal to zero and solve the two simple linear equations that result. The solutions are called the **roots** of the equation and are where the graph of y = ax² + bx + c crosses the x-axis.

bullets: Only cancel **factors that multiply** the whole numerator and the whole denominator. You cannot cancel the x in (x + 3)/(x + 2).
Factorise first, cancel second. Cancelling before factorising is a classic way to lose all the marks.
A common factor in the numerator, such as 4x + 8 over 6, simplifies to 4(x + 2)/6 = 2(x + 2)/3.
When adding or subtracting fractions, factorising the denominators first helps to find the lowest common denominator.
State any value of x which would make the denominator zero if the question asks for restrictions.
core.h: Simplifying algebraic fractions by factorising (Higher tier)
core.p: To simplify an **algebraic fraction**, factorise the numerator and the denominator completely and then **cancel common factors** (whole brackets or whole factors, never single terms from inside a sum). This is the most common place where factorising is tested after solving equations, and it appears in Higher-tier questions worth 3 to 4 marks. The answer must be fully simplified, so look for every possible factor, including differences of two squares in the numerator or denominator.

bullets: Show that (2n + 1)² − (2n − 1)² is a multiple of 8: this is a difference of two squares, so = (2n + 1 + 2n − 1)(2n + 1 − 2n + 1) = 4n × 2 = **8n**, which is a multiple of 8.
Show that n² + n is always even: n² + n = n(n + 1), which is a product of two consecutive integers; one of them is even, so the product is even.
Show that the sum of any three consecutive integers is a multiple of 3: n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = **3(n + 1)**.
Show that (n + 3)² − (n − 3)² = 12n by expanding or by the difference of two squares: (2n)(6) = 12n.
Always finish with a sentence: 'which is a multiple of 8, so the statement is true for all integers n'.
Examiners award the final mark only for a clear **factor shown** and a **conclusion**.
core.p: Factorising is the main tool for **algebraic proof**, in which you show that a statement is true for every integer, not just for examples. Write general numbers using n (such as 2n for an even number and 2n + 1 for an odd number), expand or factorise, and show that the result must contain a particular factor such as 8 or 4. A proof must end with a **clear conclusion**, and testing a few numbers never counts as proof.

bullets: Signs: in x² − 5x − 14 the numbers are −7 and +2, not +7 and −2. Always check that the **sum** gives the sign of b.
Do not stop at a partly factorised answer: 2(x² − 4) must continue to 2(x + 2)(x − 2).
Link to **graphs**: the roots of y = (x − 3)(x + 2) are where y = 0, i.e. x = 3 and x = −2.
Link to **geometry**: area and perimeter expressions are often factorised, for example an area of x² + 5x + 6 can be a rectangle with sides (x + 2) and (x + 3).
Link to **surds and rationalising**: the difference of two squares is used to rationalise denominators like 1/(√3 + 1), which is multiplied by (√3 − 1)/(√3 − 1) to give (√3 − 1)/2.
Link to **calculus** (beyond GCSE): factorised form shows the roots at a glance.
core.h: Common errors, checks and link to other topics
core.p: Nearly all lost marks in factorising come from **sign errors**, **stopping too early**, or **not checking**. Build the habit of expanding your answer mentally or on the side of the page. Factorising is connected to many other topics, so your accuracy here pays off across Algebra, Graphs and Geometry. Treat it as a skill to be practised to automatic level.

exam: **'Factorise' (1 to 2 marks):** common factor questions are often 2 marks: 1 mark for a partial factorisation (e.g. 3(2x² − 3xy)), 1 mark for the fully factorised answer 3x(2x − 3y).
**x² + bx + c (2 marks):** M1 for brackets that give the correct x² term and one correct other term (or a correct pair of numbers), A1 for both brackets correct.
**Difference of two squares (2 marks):** write (a)² − (b)² to show the method, then (a + b)(a − b). Mention 'difference of two squares' if you have space.
**ax² + bx + c (3 marks):** show the split of the middle term or the trial brackets; method marks are given for a correct pair that multiplies to ac.
**'Solve' by factorising (3 marks):** rearrange to equal zero, factorise, state both roots. Do not give only one root.
**'Show that' or proof (3 to 4 marks):** show the algebra line by line, state the factor you have found (such as 8n) and write a conclusion in words.
**Algebraic fractions (3 marks):** factorise numerator and denominator (1 mark each), then cancel and state the simplified fraction.
Always **expand to check** your answer, writing the check beside your working.
Command words: 'factorise' means a product; 'expand' means a sum; 'solve' means find values of x; 'simplify' for fractions means factorise and cancel.
Graph link: the question may give the graph and the factorised equation. The roots are the x-intercepts, so read them directly.
Never leave a blank: partial factorisations still earn the first method mark.

mistakes.r: Take out the highest common factor: 6(x + 2). Fully factorised is needed for full marks.
The pair must add to −5 and multiply to −14: (x − 7)(x + 2). Expand to check.
x² + 9 does not factorise; only x² − 9 is a difference of two squares. Expanding (x + 3)² gives x² + 6x + 9.
4x + 4x² = 4x(1 + x). A term that equals the common factor leaves 1.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the 1 left in the bracket, e.g. 4x + 4x² = 4x(x)

mistakes.r: Rearrange to x² − 5x = 0, factorise x(x − 5) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 5.
mistakes.w: Solving x² = 5x by dividing by x, leaving only x = 5

mistakes.r: Make one side zero first: x² + 2x − 15 = 0, then (x + 5)(x − 3) = 0.
mistakes.w: Factorising x² + 2x = 15 as x(x + 2) = 15, so x = 15 or x + 2 = 15

mistakes.r: Only cancel common factors of the whole numerator and whole denominator after factorising.
mistakes.w: Cancelling the x in (x + 3)/(x + 2) or cancelling terms in a sum

mistakes.r: (x + k)² = x² + 2kx + k²; the middle term must not be missed.
Expanding the brackets mentally takes seconds and catches nearly all sign errors.

summary: You must be able to factorise expressions fully: taking out common factors, factorising quadratics of the form x² + bx + c (including the difference of two squares) and, at Higher tier, ax² + bx + c. It matters because factorising is the key to solving quadratic equations, simplifying algebraic fractions, proving statements and reading roots from graphs.

terms.d: A number, letter or expression that divides exactly into another expression.
Write an expression as a product of two or more factors, usually using brackets.
An expression written as a product in which no bracket still contains a common factor.
A factor that divides exactly into every term of an expression.
The largest number or term that is a factor of every term.
Multiply out brackets to give a sum of terms; the inverse of factorising.
An expression whose highest power of the variable is 2, written ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0.
The number multiplying a variable, such as 7 in 7x.
The term with no variable, such as c in ax² + bx + c.
An expression with two terms, such as x + 3.
An expression of the form a² − b², which factorises to (a + b)(a − b).
A quadratic of the form (x + k)² = x² + 2kx + k².
A value of x that makes the expression or equation equal zero.
If the product of two factors is zero, then at least one factor is zero.
An equation true for all values of the variable, shown by the symbol ≡.
A fraction whose numerator or denominator contains algebraic terms.
